title: What lies below the waterline of sustainable AI skills · hancrafted
description: When a task you keep explaining should become a skill, how to write its description as the moment you'd need it, what goes into the skill and what stays in project context, and what a shared skill needs to stay right: an owner, a version, tests and a retirement date.

Stays the same every run grill-with-docs Skill · runs two skills: the grilling interview and domain-modeling grill-with-docs/SKILL.md Call the Skill tool twice, for "grilling" and "domain-modeling". Skill · the interview grilling/SKILL.md Map the plan as a tree of decisions. Map this as a design tree. Ask every question you can ask now, in one round. Ask the whole frontier in one round … Recommend an answer to each. … give your recommended answer. Wait for your answers, then go on. Then wait for the user's answers … Skill · domain-modeling domain-modeling/SKILL.md Check words against the glossary. ### Challenge against the glossary Sharpen fuzzy words. ### Sharpen fuzzy language Write terms down as they settle. ### Update GLOSSARY.md inline Record hard-to-reverse decisions. ### Offer ADRs sparingly runs runs again, same steps Run 1 Monday · writes its files beside the skill /grill-with-docs writes GLOSSARY.md , docs/adr/ Glossary GLOSSARY.md Project terms # Glossary Site : One sampling point on the seabed. A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:31 You are the captain Imagine you work with an AI model that is brilliant at its job, the most capable colleague you have. I will give it a picture, because we need one all the way down: you are the captain of a coastal research project, and the model is your pilot of ten years, who steers a diving robot on a cable from the control room on deck while you decide where the project goes next. 0:31 – 0:53 One settled condition Your pilot has one condition, and it never changes. He forms no new memories overnight, but he keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot, every rule of the trade. That is an AI model: what it learnt in training stays, and what you told it in yesterday's conversation is gone.

What a skill is 0:00 – 0:23 Surface first We are still at the surface, so before we ask when to write a skill, let's see what a skill is made of. I'll use the words your chat app uses, and if you work with a coding agent, some Slides have a second view that shows you the files behind each part. 0:23 – 0:39 The mechanics, plainly I want to be exact about how a skill gets loaded, because everything later depends on it. So I say first what the AI really does, and use the dive only to make it easier to picture.

When to write one 0:00 – 0:14 Sunlight We are one level down, in the sunlit zone. Here we decide two things: when a task deserves a skill at all, and how to describe it so the model actually picks it. 0:14 – 0:31 Borrowed principles From here on I borrow principles from engineering, information architecture and UX, and they all lean on one idea: what works for people also works for AI. I say that as a strong rule of thumb, not as a law. 0:31 – 0:52 Why a rule of thumb It holds because the model acts only on what you hand it, like a capable newcomer on their first day. It is only a rule of thumb because there are places where it breaks, and I've put those in the notes on the next Slide for you to read.

The description 0:00 – 0:12 The label decides We are still in sunlight, and this is the part most people skip. A skill the model never picks helps nobody, so the description matters more than the instructions. 0:12 – 0:26 Name, description Before the model opens a skill, it sees two lines: the name and the description. That is all the index holds, and it is all the model has to decide with.

What context goes inside 0:00 – 0:13 Twilight Deeper now, into the twilight zone, where the light is dim. The skill is written and described, and the question is what context goes into it and what stays beside it. 0:13 – 0:28 A decision, not a law I want to be careful with the word rule here. Keeping the procedure apart from project details is a design decision with trade-offs on both sides, so I'll show you the trade-offs and you decide.

What context stays beside 0:00 – 0:15 Beside, not inside Now the other home: project details that stay outside the skill, in project files it reads when it runs. The procedure goes inside, and whatever changes from one project to the next stays beside. 0:15 – 0:29 Where it gets shared And who uses the skill decides how much care it needs. A skill for your own use can be loose, and a skill a colleague runs needs more, which sets up the next Section.

Beside the skill 0:00 – 0:21 The card points Here is the mistake from before, fixed. The skill no longer says 40 metres. Its step says "descend to the depth in today's dive plan", and that dive plan is a project file the skill reads when the step runs: site 4, 40 metres, site 7, 120 metres. 0:21 – 0:41 Same card, any site Replay site 7. It is the same skill with no edit, and this time the robot reaches the seabed at 120 metres. The procedure stayed put and the site details lived in the project file, which is your third step in miniature: decide where the project details live. 0:41 – 0:58 For developers In the coding-agent view the step names a project file, say CONTEXT.md, and the agent reads it when that step runs. For everyone else, it is any document in your project that the skill tells the model to read.

Who uses it, and where 0:00 – 0:12 Two questions Here is a decision tool, and it asks two questions. Who uses the skill, only you or others too? And where, in any project or in one in particular? 0:12 – 0:48 Four squares Four squares come out of that. Personal and project-specific: write the details straight in, it needs the least upkeep. Personal and general: keep the details beside, it is your own toolkit. Shared and project-specific: the details can live in its supporting files, and the project team owns it. Shared and general: the details sit beside, with an owner, a version and evals. So as a skill moves from your own notebook into the shared library, it loses its project details and gains an owner. 0:48 – 1:02 A rule of thumb This matrix is a rule of thumb, and the label is mine. It is how I think about it, so try it on your own skills and tell me where it breaks.

grill-with-docs keeps context beside the skill 0:00 – 0:18 The interview is the card Let me show you inside and beside together, on real files instead of the dive. This is grill-with-docs, a skill by Matt Pocock that I use, and it runs an interview, which is the procedure. It stays the same every time. 0:18 – 0:33 Follow the arrow While it runs, grill-with-docs writes files beside itself, a glossary and decision records, and the next run checks your words against them. The skill stays the same, and what it learned about your project waits beside it. 0:33 – 0:47 Skills can run skills One last thing: a skill can also run other skills: grill-with-docs runs one called grilling and another called domain-modeling. There is no settled name for that yet, and I'll leave it there.

Sharing it 0:00 – 0:10 Midnight Now we are in deep water, the midnight zone. Everything so far was for you, so what changes when a colleague runs your skill? 0:10 – 0:22 Three jobs Three jobs wait down here. Give the skill an owner and a version, decide who looks after the shared library, and test that the skill actually helps.

Keeping it alive 0:00 – 0:09 The Abyss This is the deepest zone, the abyss, months later. Writing the skill was quick, and keeping it right is the work. 0:09 – 0:20 Nobody sees it Most people stop at the first good run, and the part below it gets little attention, which is why I want to spend three Slides here.
